facts.summary: North Dakota's minimum wage is $7.25 per hour, the same as the federal minimum wage.
facts.sourceAgency: North Dakota Legislative Branch (North Dakota Century Code)
facts.notes: Set at $7.25 effective July 24, 2009 and unchanged since; follows federal $7.25. The commissioner may adopt a different rate by rule (34-06-22(2)), so verify the current administrative rate periodically. N.D.C.C. 34-06-23 bars political subdivisions from enacting a local minimum/living wage above the state rate.

facts.summary: North Dakota requires overtime at 1.5x the regular rate only after 40 hours in a week, with no daily overtime and no state salary threshold higher than federal.
facts.citation: N.D. Admin. Code 46-02-07-02(4) (Minimum Wage and Work Conditions Order)
facts.sourceAgency: North Dakota Department of Labor and Human Rights (Administrative Code)
facts.notes: Overtime is computed weekly (excess of 40 hours). No daily overtime provision and no higher state exempt-salary floor was found, so the federal FLSA salary level ($684/week) controls. Section number for the overtime subsection is approximate; the requirement text is confirmed.

value: status with regard to marriage (marital status)
status with regard to public assistance
participation in lawful activity off the employer's premises during nonworking hours (lawful off-duty conduct)
facts.summary: Beyond the federal characteristics, North Dakota's Human Rights Act protects marital status, status with regard to public assistance, and participation in lawful off-duty activity outside work.
facts.sourceAgency: North Dakota Legislative Branch (North Dakota Century Code)
facts.notes: The Act also lists race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age (40+), and physical or mental disability, matching federal categories. The three listed here are the additions beyond the federal set.

facts.summary: North Dakota's Human Rights Act covers employers with one or more employees, far broader than the federal 15-employee threshold under Title VII/ADA.
facts.sourceAgency: North Dakota Legislative Branch (North Dakota Century Code)
facts.notes: Employer means a person within the state who employs one or more employees for more than one quarter of the year (or whose employees' services are partly/wholly performed in ND). This is a significant expansion over federal coverage for small employers.

facts.summary: An employment discrimination complaint must be filed with the ND Department of Labor and Human Rights (or an action brought in district court) within 300 days of the alleged discriminatory act.
facts.sourceAgency: North Dakota Legislative Branch (North Dakota Century Code)
facts.notes: The 300-day period applies to employment (and credit) claims; a shorter 180-day period applies to public-service/public-accommodation claims (14-02.4-19(1)). Matches the federal 300-day EEOC deadline in deferral states.

facts.value: prohibited under the Human Rights Act
facts.summary: It is an unlawful discriminatory practice to retaliate against a person who opposed discrimination or filed, testified in, or participated in a proceeding under the Human Rights Act.
facts.sourceAgency: North Dakota Legislative Branch (North Dakota Century Code)
facts.notes: Covers threats, retaliation, or discrimination for opposing an unlawful practice or good-faith participation in an investigation, hearing, or litigation. Enforced through the same complaint process and deadlines as other Human Rights Act claims.

facts.value: private and public employees protected for reporting suspected legal violations
facts.summary: North Dakota's whistleblower statute bars any employer from discharging, disciplining, or penalizing an employee for good-faith reporting of a suspected violation of law, participating in a public investigation, or refusing an order the employee reasonably believes is illegal.
facts.sourceAgency: North Dakota Legislative Branch (North Dakota Century Code)
facts.notes: A civil action for reinstatement, back pay (up to 2 years), injunctive relief, and attorney's fees must be brought within 180 days of the violation (or completion of applicable proceedings). Alternatively a complaint may be filed with the Department of Labor and Human Rights within 300 days. Applies broadly to private and public employers, unlike many states' state-employee-only laws.

facts.summary: Suits to recover unpaid wages, overtime, damages, fees, or penalties must be brought within two years after the claim accrues.
facts.sourceAgency: North Dakota Legislative Branch (North Dakota Century Code)
facts.notes: Covers actions under the FLSA and 'all other similar acts' respecting payment of wages. The period is tolled while a wage claim is pending with the Labor Commissioner (34-14-08.1(3)).

facts.summary: North Dakota voids nearly all employee non-compete agreements: a contract restraining anyone from exercising a lawful profession, trade, or business is void to that extent, with narrow exceptions for the sale of a business's goodwill and for partners/members/shareholders upon or in anticipation of dissolving a partnership, LLC, or similar entity. North Dakota courts apply the statute strictly with no judicially created reasonableness exception and no authority to narrow (blue-pencil) an overbroad covenant.
facts.sourceAgency: North Dakota Legislative Branch (North Dakota Century Code)
facts.notes: This statute traces to the Dakota Territory's 1865 adoption of the Field Civil Code and predates statehood. Unlike California's parallel rule, North Dakota's exceptions are limited to the sale-of-goodwill and dissolution scenarios; ordinary employer/employee non-compete restraints are void with no reasonableness test.

facts.value: due on the next regular payday established in advance
facts.summary: On discharge, voluntary separation, or suspension, an employee's unpaid wages become due on the regular paydays the employer set in advance for the periods worked; there is no immediate final-pay requirement.
facts.sourceAgency: North Dakota Legislative Branch (North Dakota Century Code)
facts.notes: When an employer discharges an employee it must send those wages by certified mail to the employee's designated address or as otherwise agreed. Federal law has no final-pay timing rule, so this is a state addition (though less onerous than states requiring immediate payment).
